title: The council of Jerusalem (Acts 15)
hook: a great argument: must Gentiles become Jews? they decide not to trouble them
carry: it seemed good to the spirit and us

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve and the stories tradition kept, and your line was they went everywhere.

Antioch, a big city in Syria, has a growing church where Gentiles, people who aren't Jewish, have been joining. Then visitors arrive from Judaea with a hard message: "Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved." The letter later says these visitors "went out from us," from the church in Jerusalem. Their question is honest: if Gentiles are joining the people of Israel's God, shouldn't they keep Israel's covenant? Paul and Barnabas disagree, loudly. The text calls it "no small dissension and disputation." Nobody can settle it in Antioch, so the church sends Paul, Barnabas and some others up to Jerusalem.

Acts fifteen is a meeting, and it reads like one: "And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter." There's much disputing. Then Peter stands up and tells what he saw: God giving the Holy Spirit to Gentiles, with no difference made. He ends: "we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they." Notice the direction. Not they, like us. We, like them. The room goes quiet and listens to Barnabas and Paul tell what they saw among the Gentiles. Then James, whom Paul elsewhere calls "James the Lord's brother," sums it up: "my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God." Instead they send a short letter asking a few things: keep away from food offered to idols, from blood, from what's strangled, from sexual immorality. Some readers hear in that list the old rules for strangers living among Israel. And the letter gives today's line: "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things." The Holy Spirit, and us; not one without the other. The decision came out of argument, testimony, scripture and listening, and they still spoke as people trying to follow God rather than win. Some churches still turn to this chapter when they disagree. When the letter is read in Antioch, "they rejoiced for the consolation." A fight, settled, and the people who received it were glad.

Bring to mind one disagreement that's still open, at home, at work, in a club or a church, and notice what you've been asking of the other side. Then ask the council's question: what's actually necessary here, and what one burden could you set down and let them keep their way? If you pray, bring the quarrel to God as it is.
James. The Lord's brother, whose sentence at the Jerusalem council was not to trouble Gentile believers with more than the necessary things.
Your line: it seemed good to the spirit and us. No greater burden than the necessary things. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Churches have looked to Acts 15 as a pattern for settling disagreements: meeting together, hearing what people have seen, reading scripture, and seeking the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

fork.setup: you're James. the room has argued, Peter has spoken, Paul and Barnabas have told what they saw. everyone looks at you. what do you say?
options: Gentile believers must keep the whole law of Moses.
trouble them not; ask only the necessary things.
send everyone home and let each church decide.
fork.reveal: "my sentence is, that we trouble not them." a short letter goes out, and in Antioch they rejoice.

chat.says: At the Jerusalem council, did Gentile believers have to keep all of Moses' law?
options: No: James said don't trouble them, and asked only a few necessary things.
Yes, the council said they had to be circumcised before they could join.
No, the council asked them for nothing at all, and sent no letter.
chat.meaning: James' sentence was not to trouble Gentile believers; the letter laid on them no greater burden than a few necessary things.

Antioch.meaning: a big city in Syria with a growing church

Barnabas.meaning: Paul's companion at Antioch and at the council

Holy Ghost.meaning: an older English name for the Holy Spirit

notes: Editor pass: 'these visitors are believers' replaced with the text's own 'went out from us' (15:24); James now identified by Paul's phrase in Galatians 1:19; 'ever since' softened to 'some churches still'; trapdoor's lexical claim about edoxen cut; myth item reworded to match the text.
The index hook says 'the first big argument'; the script avoids the superlative ('a great argument' in the hook field). Confirm the index hook may be softened.
The Judaean visitors and the believing Pharisees (15:1, 15:5) are presented fairly as believers with an honest covenant question, never as a foil. Confirm the tone.

James is described as 'the brother of Jesus and a leader of the Jerusalem church'. Catholic and Orthodox traditions understand 'brother' differently (cousin or step-brother); consider 'James, called the brother of the Lord' if preferred.
'Some readers hear in that list the old rules for strangers living among Israel' refers to the common link to Leviticus 17–18; attributed to 'some readers'.
The four requests summarize 15:20 and 15:29 ('fornication' rendered 'sexual immorality').
Original: ἔδοξεν (Acts 15:28, ἔδοξεν γὰρ τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ καὶ ἡμῖν). The trapdoor's 'a word used for public decisions' is a lexical claim; confirm or cut.

Second editor pass: 'growing fast, mostly with people who aren't Jewish' softened (no proportion in the text); unsourced 'they take the scriptures seriously' cut; practice's 'group chat' replaced (used on day 740).

Audit pass: 'they all go up to Jerusalem' corrected to the text (Acts 15:2: Paul, Barnabas and certain others are sent). The earlier note about 'the brother of Jesus' is stale: the script uses Paul's own phrase from Galatians 1:19.
